newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian building collapses, death toll rises to six.
newsitem.headline: Indian building collapses, death toll rises to six.

text.p: Rescue workers, struggling on Tuesday to reach people trapped under the debris of a collapsed building in Bombay, recovered a further five bodies from the debris, raising the death toll to six.

"There could be more than 25 people still trapped inside," Chief Fire Officer D.J. Kulkarni of the Bombay Fire Brigade told Reuters. "Ten people were taken to hospital with injuries. There are six dead."
Fire officials said the building, divided into apartments and offices in a dense cluster of old residential structures in India's commercial capital, collapsed shortly after noon.
It was not immediately known why it came down.
"It collapsed like a pack of cards," said T.L. D'Souza, 60, who works in a garage nearby. "Suddenly it fell. Within five minutes it was down -- flattened. No noise, no shouts for help."
The search for survivors was hampered by a lack of space to bring in heavy machinery to clear the debris, fire officials said.
"The road is too narrow to bring in bulldozers or machines," said one fire official. "We have to do the clearance by hand."
Queues of policemen and relief workers lined the narrow alley leading to the building.
Men standing on a 30-foot (nine metre) high pile of rubble passed furniture and bits of debris from hand to hand. At the end of the lines, other workmen stacked them in a nearby street.
"We can hear the voices of people faintly," said one of the firemen. "They are giving us responses."
Fire chief Kulkarni estimated it would take at least three hours to clear the rest of the rubble.
He said: "Because of the constraints of space, we cannot bring in machines to do it swiftly."
A group of residents huddled in a corner, watching the rescue operations. They said the building was old, but looked sturdy.
"A neighbour called me at work to say the building was swaying and about to fall," said Hilda Furtado, who said she had lived in the building for over 40 years.
Many of Bombay's buildings are in poor shape because city laws have frozen rents at 40-year-old levels and landlords find little financial incentive to maintain them.
Weakened by wind and heavy rains in the monsoons, many of them collapse each year.

Civic officials estimate that more than 20,000 buildings in the city are in danger of imminent collapse because of poor maintenance. But many residents have refused to move out because they have nowhere else to go to.
The building housed a printing press on the ground floor with apartments, courier agencies, tailoring shops, and a lawyer's office on the upper floors.
